new-zealand.text: A South Pacific island country with a mostly maritime climate, best known for Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc and, more recently, cool-climate Pinot Noir. Sauvignon Blanc covers about 65% of the vineyard area, followed by Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Pinot Gris. Wines are usually labeled by single grape.

new-zealand/auckland.text: A geographical indication on the North Island, around New Zealand's largest city, covering the greater Auckland Region. It has 660 acres of vines, where Chardonnay and Syrah lead the plantings, followed by Merlot and Pinot Gris. Matakana, Kumeu and Waiheke Island lie inside it.

new-zealand/bannockburn.text: A geographical indication in Central Otago, on New Zealand's South Island. New Zealand is known for its cool-climate Pinot Noir.

new-zealand/canterbury.text: A South Island geographical indication covering the whole Canterbury Region except the Kaikoura District, about 17,200 square miles.

new-zealand/central-hawke-s-bay.text: A geographical indication on New Zealand's North Island, within the wider Hawke's Bay area. Hawke's Bay grows Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc most, each about 22% of its vines, then Merlot at 20% and Pinot Gris.

new-zealand/central-otago.text: A South Island geographical indication and one of the world's southernmost wine regions. Pinot Noir is its best-known wine and covers about 81% of the vines. Pinot Gris, Chardonnay and Riesling make up most of the rest.

new-zealand/gisborne.text: A geographical indication on New Zealand's North Island where white grapes lead. Chardonnay is the main grape at 43% of the vines, followed by Sauvignon Blanc at 26% and Pinot Gris at 21%. Pinot Noir and Merlot are small plantings.

new-zealand/gladstone.text: A geographical indication on New Zealand's North Island, in the wider Wairarapa area.

new-zealand/hawkes-bay.text: One of New Zealand's oldest wine regions and its second-largest, on the North Island's east coast. Vineyards sit on the plains and low hills around Napier and Hastings. Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc lead at 22% each, with Merlot at 20%, so reds and whites both matter.

new-zealand/marlborough.text: New Zealand's largest wine region, in the north-east of the South Island, with about three quarters of national production and most of its exports. Sauvignon Blanc covers about 82% of the vines, and its wines are called some of the best of that style in the world. Pinot Noir is a distant second, and vineyards cluster around Blenheim and Seddon.

new-zealand/martinborough.text: A geographical indication on New Zealand's North Island, in the wider Wairarapa area. New Zealand is known for premium cool-climate Pinot Noir from Martinborough.

new-zealand/nelson.text: A geographical indication on New Zealand's South Island where Sauvignon Blanc is the main grape, at 58% of the vines. Pinot Noir follows at 14%, then Pinot Gris and Chardonnay at 11% and 10%, with a little Riesling.

new-zealand/north-canterbury.text: A geographical indication in the Canterbury region of New Zealand's South Island. Sauvignon Blanc and Pinot Noir lead at 30% and 28% of the vines. Riesling is a strong third at 18%, followed by Pinot Gris.

new-zealand/north-island.text: An enduring geographical indication covering the North Island's wine areas, from Northland and Auckland down to Hawke's Bay, Gisborne and Wairarapa. Sauvignon Blanc and Chardonnay lead at about 24% and 23% of the vines, with Pinot Gris, Merlot and Pinot Noir behind.

new-zealand/northland.text: A geographical indication on New Zealand's North Island where Chardonnay leads at 26% of the vines. Syrah follows at 19% and Pinot Gris at 14%, with smaller plantings of Merlot, Pinotage and Viognier.

new-zealand/south-island.text: An enduring geographical indication covering the South Island's wine areas, including Marlborough, Nelson, Canterbury and Central Otago. It is dominated by Sauvignon Blanc at about 74% of the vines, with Pinot Noir at 14%.

new-zealand/waiheke-island.text: A geographical indication on an island that sits within the Auckland area.

new-zealand/waipara-valley.text: A wine and tourism district on the Waipara River in Canterbury, about 37 miles north of Christchurch.

new-zealand/wairarapa.text: A geographical indication on New Zealand's North Island where Pinot Noir leads at 48% of the vines and Sauvignon Blanc follows at 37%. Chardonnay, Pinot Gris and Riesling are small plantings.

new-zealand/waitaki-valley-north-otago.text: A small, young South Island region registered as a geographical indication in 2018, with commercial planting from 2001. Limestone slopes, river gravels and a cool Pacific-influenced climate shape its Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris, Chardonnay and Riesling, known for freshness and restrained structure.

germany.text: Mainly a white wine country along the Rhine and its tributaries, known above all for Riesling, which makes wines from crisp and dry to sweet and intensely aromatic. Riesling is the top grape at 23% of vines. Red wine is a bit over a third of plantings, led by Spätburgunder (Pinot Noir).

germany/ahr.text: One of Germany's smaller wine regions, in the Ahr valley, a tributary of the Rhine. Despite its northern position it mostly makes red wine, with red grapes on 86% of its vines, more than in any other German region. Pinot Noir covers about 63% of the area.

germany/baden.text: Germany's third-largest wine region, in the southwest, and less known abroad than its size suggests. Winemaking cooperatives are very common and produce 85% of its wine. Pinot Noir leads at 36% of the vines, then Müller-Thurgau, Pinot Gris and Pinot Blanc.

germany/burgstadter-berg.text: A Franken site around the commune of Bürgstadt.

germany/franken.text: Germany's wine region in Bavaria, covering about 15,000 acres of vines in 2024. It is the only wine region in that state. Müller-Thurgau and Silvaner lead the plantings at 27% and 23%, with Bacchus third.

germany/monzinger-niederberg.text: A single site around the commune of Monzingen, in the Nahe area. Its rules allow Riesling only, as a still wine.

germany/mosel.text: A region along the Mosel, Saar and Ruwer rivers known for steep vineyard slopes above the water, including the world's steepest recorded vineyard, Bremmer Calmont. Riesling is its famous grape, at 61% of vines. Northerly Rieslings are often light, lower in alcohol, crisp and high in acidity.

germany/nahe.text: A Rhineland-Palatinate region along the River Nahe, with 75% white grapes and Riesling the leading variety. Its soils are very varied because of volcanic origins. Its Rieslings are rated highly by critics and seen as on a par with the best of Mosel and Rheingau.

germany/pfalz.text: Germany's second-largest wine region, with about 58,560 acres under vine in 2022 and some 6,800 vintners. Known as Rheinpfalz before 1993. Riesling leads the plantings at 24%, followed by the red Dornfelder at 14%, with Müller-Thurgau and Pinot Noir behind.

germany/rheingau.text: A small region in Hesse, only 3% of German vineyard area, with a higher share of Riesling than any other region, about 79% of vines. Spätburgunder (Pinot Noir) makes up most of the rest. It has been the source of many important innovations in German winemaking, and is home to Schloss Johannisberg.

germany/rheinhessen.text: Germany's largest wine region, on the left bank of the Rhine between Worms and Bingen. It makes mostly white wine from Riesling, Müller-Thurgau and Silvaner and is best known as the home of Liebfraumilch. Some Rieslings are made in a powerful dry style.

germany/uhlen-blaufusser-lay.text: A Mosel site in the commune of Winningen. Its rules allow still and sparkling wine from Riesling only.

germany/uhlen-laubach.text: A Mosel site in the commune of Winningen. Its rules allow still and sparkling wine from Riesling only.

germany/uhlen-roth-lay.text: A Mosel site spanning the communes of Kobern-Gondorf and Winningen. Its rules allow still and sparkling wine from Riesling only.

germany/wurttemberg.text: Germany's fourth-largest wine region, in the southwest, with a long history of red wine, though from different grapes than other regions. Schiava Grossa leads at 20% of vines, then Riesling, Blaufränkisch and Pinot Meunier. Cooperatives make almost 75% of its wine.

germany/wurzburger-stein-berg.text: A Franken site in the commune of Würzburg. Its rules allow still wine from Grüner Silvaner and Weißer Burgunder, with Riesling as a minor grape.

united-kingdom.text: A minor grower of wine, most of it English sparkling wine from southern England. Vineyards are becoming common in counties such as Essex, Sussex and Kent, where the climate is drier and warmer. Bacchus leads the plantings at 32%, followed by Chardonnay at 27% and the Pinots.

united-kingdom/darnibole.text: A UK protected designation of origin for wine from Cornwall. Its rules allow wine, with Bacchus as the named grape. Most UK wine is English sparkling wine, from vineyards across southern England.

united-kingdom/english.text: A protected designation of origin covering England, for still and quality sparkling wine. Its rules list many grapes, including Bacchus, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Pinot Meunier, Solaris and Rondo, across a long list of English local authorities.

united-kingdom/english-regional.text: A protected geographical indication (PGI) for English wine, one of two regional PGIs in the United Kingdom. Most UK wine is English sparkling wine, from vineyards across southern England, in counties such as Essex, Sussex and Kent.

united-kingdom/pgis.text: The group of United Kingdom protected geographical indications, holding two regional categories, one Welsh and one English. Most UK wine is English sparkling wine, from vineyards across southern England.

united-kingdom/sussex.text: A protected designation of origin for wine from the historic county of Sussex in southern England, granted in 2022. It makes more wine than any other UK county, 28% of the national total in 2023. Its sparkling wine in particular is compared with Champagne.

united-kingdom/welsh.text: A protected designation of origin covering Wales, for still and quality sparkling wine. Its rules list many grapes, including Bacchus, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Pinot Meunier, Solaris and Rondo, across the Welsh local authorities.

united-kingdom/welsh-regional.text: A protected geographical indication (PGI) for Welsh wine, one of two regional PGIs in the United Kingdom. UK wine growing has long been held back by a cool climate, but warmer summers and better-suited grapes have increased investment.

china.text: Wine has a long history here, though it was overshadowed by huangjiu and baijiu. Consumption has grown sharply since the 1980s, making China a top ten wine market. Cabernet Sauvignon leads the plantings at 23%, then Merlot and Carmenère, and Ningxia wines have won international recognition.

china/helanshan-dong-lu-pu-tao-jiu.text: A protected geographical indication (PGI) for wine in China, one of four Chinese PGIs. Wine consumption in China has grown dramatically since the 1980s, and China is now among the top ten global wine markets.

china/huanren-bing-jiu.text: A protected geographical indication (PGI) for wine in China, one of four Chinese PGIs. Wine consumption in China has grown dramatically since the 1980s, and China is now among the top ten global wine markets.

china/pgis.text: The group of Chinese protected geographical indications, which holds four: Shacheng, Yantai, Huanren Bing Jiu and Helanshan Dong Lu. China is now among the top ten global wine markets.

china/shacheng-pu-tao-jiu.text: A protected geographical indication (PGI) for wine in China, one of four Chinese PGIs. Wine consumption in China has grown dramatically since the 1980s, and China is now among the top ten global wine markets.

china/yantai-pu-tao-jiu.text: A protected geographical indication (PGI) for wine in China, one of four Chinese PGIs. Wine consumption in China has grown dramatically since the 1980s, and China is now among the top ten global wine markets.

hungary.text: A country with a long wine history, best known abroad for Tokaji aszú, a white dessert wine, and for the red Bull's Blood of Eger (Egri Bikavér). Its top plantings are Blaufränkisch at 11%, then Bianca, Cserszegi Fűszeres, Welschriesling and Furmint.

hungary/tokaj.text: A historic region of 27 named villages in northeastern Hungary, with a small part across the border in Slovakia. It is famous as the origin of Tokaji aszú, one of the world's oldest botrytized wines. Furmint covers about 65% of the vines, with Hárslevelű at 20%.
